content:
**Observation:**

- **Affected part**: Lower stem and whole plant, near soil line (black plastic mulch visible)
- **Stem**: Bleached/whitish-tan, rough-textured, completely collapsed and girdled — the plant has fallen over
- **Leaves**: Extensive brown, withered, dead tissue throughout; some green leaves still visible at the periphery
- **Location of damage**: Base/lower stem area, characteristic of a soilborne or crown pathogen
- **Notable**: Stem appears hardened and bleached rather than dark/necrotic; possible darker structures (sclerotia?) on the stem surface

**Reasoning through candidates:**

- **Southern Blight**: White cottony mycelium radiating from the base and mustard-seed-sized sclerotia — not clearly visible here
- **Sclerotinia Timber Rot**: Bleached, hardened stem with eventual collapse and plant death; sclerotia (rice-grain-sized, grayish-black) embedded in stem; white mycelium may be absent if dried. The bleached, collapsed stem near soil line fits this description well.
- **Alternaria Stem Cankers**: Dark-brown to black cankers with concentric rings — stem here is pale/bleached, not dark
- **Phytophthora/Late Blight**: Greasy dark lesions, white sporulation on undersides — not matching
- **Verticillium Wilt**: V-shaped leaf lesions, vascular discoloration — not evident here

The bleached, hardened, girdled stem causing complete plant collapse near the soil line is the hallmark of Sclerotinia Timber Rot. The absence of visible white mycelium could reflect a later/drier stage of infection.
